transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-09
Time: 11:00 AM PT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Ava Romero (Redwood CSM); Elena Torres (Head of ML, Summit Analytics), Martin Liu (Infra), Priya Desai (Security), Owen Kim (Product)

Summary (auto):
High-level discovery to understand Summit Analytics' requirements for a private/VPC deployment of Redwood Private. Focus on networking (VPC peering vs PrivateLink), region constraints, cross-account peering, CIDR allocation, egress controls, and KMS integration. Next steps: send runbook, schedule deep-dive, share network diagrams.

00:00 Jordan: hey everyone thanks for coming on time, i'm jordan with redwood, and with me is maya and ava. today we just want to understand your network constraints and what success looks like for private deployment.
00:18 Elena: thanks jordan, yeah we run a mix of batch and real-time inference. latency is important for some product features but security and data residency are top. we'll probably need redwood in our VPC or peered in a way that traffic never traverses public internet.
00:33 Maya: great, can you give a quick summary of your infra? which cloud, accounts, regions, and any compliance constraints?
00:42 Elena: primarily aws, multi-account — prod VPC in 10.1.0.0/16, infra and shared services in a separate account. our data residency requirement is us-east-1 for now, but we're evaluating us-west-2 for DR.
00:58 Martin: we also have strict egress rules, our NATs are limited and we prefer private endpoints. cross-account peering is allowed but with guardrails, and we don't do transitive peering.
01:13 Maya: ok makes sense. two main deployment patterns we typically discuss: 1) Redwood Private as a VPC-hosted service in your account with private endpoints (recommended for strict security), or 2) Redwood-managed VPC peering where we peer our service VPC to yours. both have tradeoffs.
01:31 Owen: what's the difference in egress and routing between peering and private endpoints?
01:36 Maya: with VPC peering, routing is direct at the IP level, so you can call the inference endpoint via private IPs; however peering doesn't support transitive routing so you must be explicit. PrivateLink/Interface endpoints create an ENI in your VPC and traffic goes over AWS backbone to our service — typically easier for cross-account security boundaries and avoids messing with route tables. peering can be simpler for high-throughput low-latency workloads but you need to plan CIDR overlap.
02:04 Priya: CIDR overlap is a big one for us. our prod CIDR is 10.1.0.0/16, we can't shrink that easily. do you require specific /24s on our side?
02:14 Maya: we don't require a fixed /24 but we do need non-overlapping ranges between the two VPCs if peering. if you go with PrivateLink you get an interface endpoint in your subnet so CIDR overlap isn't an issue.
02:27 Elena: what about DNS? we have internal DNS and want inference hostnames to resolve to internal IPs.
02:32 Jordan: we support giving you a private hostname that resolves to the interface endpoint IPs; with peering you'd use the private IP directly or set up conditional forwarding depending on your DNS setup. sometimes there's slight naming mismatch in transcribed docs, but we'll provide the exact steps.
02:50 Martin: what about cross-region? we want us-east-1 for prod, maybe us-west-2 DR. can you support multi-region private endpoints or peering?
02:59 Maya: yes, we can deploy regional private endpoints; for cross-region peering it's more complex. generally we recommend deploying Redwood Private in each region that you require and then replicating model state or routing at the application layer. we can also talk about active-passive failover and how KV cache warming behaves across regions — there's a latency cost if you cross regions.
03:25 Owen: KV cache — that's the cache for generation state, right? if we failover will we lose warm cache and see latency spikes?
03:31 Maya: correct, the KV cache is local to the runtime. failover to a different region will have cold caches; we have warm-up strategies and pre-warming scripts we can run as part of the runbook.
03:45 Priya: encryption — we need CMEK via our KMS, and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM. how does redwood integrate with customer-managed KMS and cloudtrail?
03:55 Jordan: we support customer KMS for key wrapping, and we can configure the private deployment to use your KMS keys. for audit logs we can forward structured logs to your logging endpoint or configure cross-account CloudWatch logs/CloudTrail ingestion. we'll include the specifics in the security pack.
04:12 Elena: SOC2 evidence and penetration testing reports?
04:16 Ava: yes, we can share SOC2 report, pen test summaries, and a security questionnaire. we'll add those to the drop and Jordan will send a pointer.
04:27 Martin: network ACLs — do you require open access to subnets? our policy is least privilege.
04:33 Maya: we recommend dedicated subnets for the interface endpoints, and security groups limiting ports to only what the runtime needs (typically HTTPS 443) and internal health checks. we won't ask you to open wide ranges. if peering, you'll control routing and security on your side.
04:51 Elena: what about egress from the runtime for model downloads, telemetry, updates — can that be locked down?
04:58 Maya: in a private deployment inside your account, model artifact fetching can happen from S3 or an internal artifact repo via VPC endpoints. telemetry can be routed to your logging endpoints. if you prefer no outbound internet at all, we can run an air-gapped variant but that adds operational overhead and a slightly longer provisioning timeline.
05:18 Owen: timeline — if we wanted to pilot in us-east-1, what's a realistic timeline?
05:22 Jordan: typical pilot: 2-4 weeks for infra setup (network configuration, IAM, cert exchange), then 1-2 weeks for model onboarding and validation, so roughly 4-6 weeks end-to-end for a focused pilot. air-gapped or on-prem can be longer.
05:40 Priya: any limits on IPs for interface endpoints or ENIs per AZ? we have quota guards in our accounts.
05:45 Maya: depends on cloud provider; on AWS you need ENI quota per AZ — we will provide recommended quotas in the runbook. for high-throughput setups we may request larger ENI counts and subnets sized to /24 to be safe.
05:58 Martin: do you support PrivateLink on GCP and Azure equivalents?
06:02 Maya: GCP has VPC peering and Private Service Connect; Azure has Private Link. we support those patterns but details differ; we'll include provider-specific steps.
06:12 Elena: how do you handle model upgrades and rollouts in private deployments? can we pin versions?
06:18 Jordan: yes you can pin model versions, and we support canary rollouts and traffic split. for private deployments we push the runtime updates via our control plane — if you're in a private control plane model (customer-managed control plane), we have an option where you have more control over updates.
06:35 Owen: billing — is there a different pricing for private/VPC?
06:38 Jordan: yes, private and dedicated typically have commitment-based pricing; we'll send a price sheet. Hosted API is usage-based. We'll include estimated egress and networking cost notes.
06:50 Priya: one more — do you support SAML SSO for the console and RBAC?
06:55 Ava: yes, SSO via SAML/OpenID Connect and role-based access controls are supported; we'll include setup steps.
07:05 Martin: curious about peering with our shared services account — we want to centralize egress/NAT. since you recommended avoiding transitive peering, is there a recommended pattern?
07:15 Maya: common pattern is to deploy interface endpoints in the application account so traffic terminates there and then you can route outbound through your shared services. Alternatively, if you want the runtime in a shared infra account, we can peer directly but you'll need explicit route entries. we'll diagram both options.
07:33 Elena: any gotchas with MTU or throughput?
07:36 Maya: not usually, but when you run GPU-heavy workloads you should provision for higher network throughput per instance. peering is IP level so you get native throughput, PrivateLink is proxied and may add a small overhead but negligible for most use cases.
07:53 Owen: are there customers running in a hybrid on-prem + cloud setup?
07:56 Maya: yes, some are running private deployments in a VPC that connect back to on-prem via Direct Connect or VPN. we support that topology; for on-prem-only air-gapped we provide an appliance packaging.
08:10 Priya: risk profile — if we do peering with your service VPC, do you require any access into our VPC for monitoring?
08:17 Jordan: no, we don't need access into your VPC. metrics and logs can be exported to your endpoints. if you want hosted managed service in our VPC we'll limit inbound policies. access is negotiable.
08:30 Elena: ok last bit — performance SLAs?
08:33 Maya: for Dedicated and Private we offer latency targets as part of SLA; specifics depend on deployment profile. for pilot we'll propose a target and measure via tracing hooks.
08:43 Jordan: wrap-up: Jordan to send pricing and runbook with recommended quotas, Maya to run technical deep dive on network patterns and a Terraform example, Priya to send CIDR and security constraints. we'll reconvene after customer's network team reviews.
08:57 Elena: perfect thanks all.
09:00 call ends
